mcqs.question: You get five minutes with a VP to cover the same Kafka migration you presented to your team last week. Which framing fits the audience?
options: "The manual backfill that cost four engineer-hours twice this quarter goes away. Three weeks of one engineer, no customer-facing change, and it unblocks analytics' replay requirement."
A walkthrough of the outbox poller batching 500 rows and the two-week dual-read cutover window
The same deck you gave the team, cut down to half the slides
A comparison of Kafka's partition model against SQS FIFO queue semantics
mcqs.explanation: A VP is deciding whether to keep funding the work, so the useful content is cost, impact, risk and what it unblocks — note the strong version names no technologies at all and is not simplified, it answers a different question. Simply shortening the team's deck is the most tempting option and the most common mistake: less of the wrong altitude is still the wrong altitude, and it makes a senior listener do the summarising you owed them.

mcqs.question: Which of these closing lines is a well-formed ask?
options: "So that's roughly where we are — any questions?"
"We'd really appreciate support from the platform team on this going forward."
"Let me know if anyone has concerns about the timeline."
"I need a yes or no on managed Kafka from Dan by Friday. If it's no, we keep the runbook and I close the RFC."
mcqs.explanation: A real ask names the person, the decision, the date, and what happens on each answer — that is what converts a presentation into an outcome. Asking for "support going forward" is the near-miss: it sounds like an ask but assigns nobody, commits nothing, and reliably produces a room full of nods and no action.

mcqs.question: Your October 3 date is now at risk. Which way of reporting that to a skip-level manager damages trust the most?
options: Leading with it: "Oct 3 is at risk, I'll know for certain Friday, here's what would hold it"
Mentioning it after four paragraphs of PR-level implementation detail and closing with "just FYI"
Saying the date is at risk and naming the one thing you'd need from them to protect it
Flagging the risk now with a date by which you'll confirm, even though it may still land on time
mcqs.explanation: Burying a slipping date under detail reads as concealment even when it was only enthusiasm, and it costs far more credibility than the slip itself would have. The other three are all defensible — flagging early and being wrong is cheap, because a senior manager's actual question is whether they will be surprised later.

mcqs.question: Thirty seconds into your live demo, staging starts returning 502s. What is the strongest move?
options: Open the logs and debug it for a couple of minutes — the room will be understanding and it demonstrates real skill
Apologise, drop the demo, and describe in words what it would have shown
Retry once, and within about twenty seconds switch to the screen recording you made yesterday, continuing at normal pace
Ask a teammate to fix staging while you move to the next section, then come back to the demo
mcqs.explanation: A prepared recording preserves the evidence the demo was there to provide and costs the room nothing — people have seen wifi die. Handing the fix to a teammate and circling back is the plausible-sounding trap: it keeps the meeting hostage to an environment problem and splits everyone's attention, while live debugging is worse still because the meeting is now about your bug rather than your decision.

mcqs.question: A senior engineer objects: "this puts a new on-call surface on SRE and you haven't costed that." The uncosted part is accurate. What is the best response in the room?
options: Explain that on-call impact is out of scope for the decision being made today
Say you'll take it offline so the meeting can stay on the agenda
Note that every migration adds operational surface, so the concern isn't specific to this proposal
Agree that the on-call surface is real and uncosted, say why you'd still accept it, and commit to a number by a named date
mcqs.explanation: Conceding the accurate half of an objection first is what lets you defend the rest credibly, and pairing it with a dated commitment converts a gap into a follow-up instead of a weakness. Deferring it offline is the tempting move because it protects the agenda, but this objection goes directly to the recommendation's cost — parking a central concern reads as evasion, which is exactly the outcome you were trying to avoid.
